info.name: Alpha Law orchestrator — API v1
info.description:
Natural-language orchestration over Gmail, Calendar and Drive.

## Read this first

**Writes are two-phase.** POST /api/v1/query only ever *prepares* an action plus the prompt that gates it. Nothing reaches Google until a person approves it through POST /api/v1/prompts/{id}/respond. The database enforces this: actions.requires_input_id is NOT NULL and references pending_inputs(id), so a confirm-requiring write cannot exist without a prompt gating it.

## Setup

1. `docker compose up`
2. Open **1 · Auth → Start Google OAuth** in a browser and complete consent.
3. Copy the `alpha_session` cookie value into the collection variable `session_token`. The collection pre-request script attaches it to every request.
4. Run the folders in order. Test scripts chain ids between requests: the query folder captures conversation_id, run_id, input_id and action_id, and the prompts folder consumes them.

## The chained flow

`Write · cancel my Turkish Airlines flight` → captures `input_id` + `action_id` → `Approve the write · Send it` → 202 and a job id → watch `action.done` on `3 · Runs`.

`Ambiguous · move the meeting with John` → captures `blocking_input_id` + `chosen_option_id` → `Answer a blocking prompt · which John` → 200 and the run resumes at 0 LLM calls.

Full prose docs, including the SSE event union and the seq gap-detection contract: `docs/API.md`. Machine-readable spec: `docs/openapi.json`.

item.name: 1 · Auth
item.description: Start here. Open 'Start Google OAuth' in a browser, complete consent, then copy the alpha_session cookie value into the collection variable `session_token`. Every other request sends it via the collection pre-request script.

request.description:
Redirects to Google's consent screen. Turn OFF 'Automatically follow redirects' in Postman settings to see the 302, or just open the URL in a browser — this is a browser flow, not an API call.

`next` must be a relative same-origin path; an absolute URL is rejected 422 (open-redirect guard).

Google's redirect target. You do not call this by hand — it is here so the collection documents every endpoint. Exchanges the code, encrypts the tokens into oauth_tokens, queues the initial backfill, sets the alpha_session cookie, and 302s to `next`.

The first call a client makes. Returns the user, the health of the Google grant, and the remaining hourly query budget. No token material, ever.

`google.needs_reauth: true` means the next query would 428 — show the reconnect banner before the user hits it.

request.description:
Revokes at Google, wipes the encrypted tokens, cancels every draft/approved action and deletes their Gmail drafts, cancels pending prompts, and (with purge=true) drops the sync_ mirror.

Conversations, messages, runs and audit rows survive — this is a disconnect, not an account deletion.

`purge=false` keeps the mirror so reconnecting does not re-backfill 180 days.

item.name: 2 · Query
item.description: The one entry point. A query only ever PREPARES a write — nothing here sends an email, moves an event or shares a file. Run 'Cancel my Turkish Airlines flight' first: its test script captures conversation_id, run_id, input_id and action_id into collection variables, which the Prompts folder then uses.

request.description: Resolves against conversation_entities — roughly 20 rows for the thread — instead of re-parsing previous runs' result blobs. Needs a conversation_id, so run one of the reads above first.

Same run, streamed. Each line is one complete JSON object in exactly the SSE envelope — {v, seq, type, run_id, ts, data}. One event union, two transports.

item.name: 3 · Runs (SSE)
item.description:
Server-sent events for one run. Read-only — opening it starts nothing.

seq gap-detection: hold last_seq (starts 0). seq == last_seq+1 → apply. seq <= last_seq → a reconnect duplicate, DROP it (content.delta appends, so applying twice corrupts the text). seq > last_seq+1 → you missed events; reconnect with Last-Event-ID and the server replays from a 500-event, 15-minute Redis buffer. Past that window you get a single `error` event with code STREAM_EXPIRED — fall back to GET /api/v1/conversations/{id}, which is the durable record.

request.description:
Fourteen event types on the run channel: run.started, progress, probe.done, intent, plan.step, step.started, step.retrying, step.finished, content.delta, token, input.raised, action.prepared, run.paused, run.complete, error. Plus action.done and action.failed, which arrive after the run itself has finished.

Postman buffers SSE rather than rendering it live. For a live view:

  curl -N '$BASE/api/v1/runs/<run_id>/events' -H 'Accept: text/event-stream' -b cookies.txt

item.name: 4 · Prompts (the write gate)
item.description:
One endpoint answers all six prompt kinds, blocking and non-blocking alike, because the validation authority is the row's own value_schema — the server runs jsonschema.validate against it and nothing else. A new prompt kind therefore needs no API change and no client release.

Run the Query folder first so input_id and blocking_input_id are populated.

request.description: Everything the system is waiting on. Each row carries its value_schema — that is the contract your card must satisfy. `options` is display only; a choice prompt's enum lives in the schema, and posting an option id absent from the enum correctly fails validation.

exec: pm.test('every prompt carries its own schema', function () {

request.description: Rows are never deleted — the status changes. That is what lets a reopened chat show a card in its answered or cancelled state rather than a frozen snapshot.

exec: pm.test('statuses come from the enum', function () {

request.description:
Stage 3-5 of the two-phase write: approve, revalidate, execute.

Six revalidation checks run in pure Python before anything is queued — prompt still pending and unexpired, value validates, action still draft, dedupe_key still unique among in-flight actions, Google grant live and scoped, target unchanged (If-Match on the calendar etag).

Returns 202: the send is handed to the Celery `actions` queue with an X-Orchestrator-Idem header, so a retry after an ambiguous timeout checks Sent before sending again. Watch for action.done on the run's stream.

pm.test('the action was queued, not executed inline', function () {

request.description:
The Edit button. approve:false plus a patch applies the change to actions.payload, appends the old payload to actions.revisions, recomputes dedupe_key, answers this prompt, and raises a NEW confirm prompt against the revised payload — returned as `next_input`.

Still 0 LLM calls: the edit came from the person, so there is nothing to plan. The Gmail draft is updated in place, so external_ref does not change and the user sees the edit in their own Drafts folder.

item.name: Answer a blocking prompt · which John

request.description:
The other half of the same endpoint. This prompt is blocking, so answering it RESUMES the paused run — 200, not 202 — and the response hands back resumed_run_id and a `watch` URL.

The seq on that stream continues from where run.paused left it, so reattach at your last_seq rather than from 1.

The value here is a bare string because this prompt's value_schema is {type: string, enum: [...]}. Nothing in the API layer knows that; jsonschema does.

exec: pm.test('resuming costs zero LLM calls', function () {

request.description:
approve:false with no patch. The prompt is answered, the action is cancelled, and the Gmail draft it created is deleted.

Because the unique index on actions.dedupe_key is PARTIAL — covering only draft, approved and running — a cancelled action does not block an identical one later. Resending after cancelling is a legitimate new request.

exec: pm.test('the action was cancelled, not sent', function () {

request.description: Dismiss without recording a decision. Cancelling a prompt that gates an action cancels the action too. Cancelling a BLOCKING prompt cancels the run — the steps that already ran keep their rows, so the trace stays intact.

Run this straight after 'Approve the write'. The double-tapped send button.

details.status tells you which terminal state it is in: answered, cancelled, expired, or superseded (a newer run prepared the same kind of write, and the old prompt was superseded in that same transaction).

item.name: 5 · Conversations
item.description: The durable record. This is what a client falls back to when an SSE stream drops past the replay window — Postgres is the source of truth, SSE is only an accelerator.

request.description:
Keyset pagination on (last_message_at, id), served by the partial index (user_id, last_message_at DESC) WHERE archived_at IS NULL.

title_is_derived:true means conversations.title IS NULL and the label shown is the first user message — nothing is stored for it.
Pass the cursor from the previous response. Opaque — do not parse it.

Messages with every ref resolved, plus runs, pending_inputs, actions and entities.

messages[].content is an ordered block list: prose inline, anything with a lifecycle by ref. Resolve each ref against the pending_inputs and actions arrays in the same response. A ref with no match was dropped on read — never render it as an empty box.

include_trace=true attaches each assistant message's node_executions. They are keyed by message_id, which is why a paused run's trace does not appear under both of its messages.
Another user's conversation returns 404, not 403. A 403 would confirm the id exists.

exec: pm.test('error envelope is the documented shape', function () {

item.name: 6 · Sync
item.description: The pgvector mirror of Gmail, Calendar and Drive. Celery beat syncs every 15 minutes, smeared with countdown = hash(user_id) % 900 so a million users do not hit Google on the same second. These endpoints force it and report where it got to.

request.description:
Advances from the stored cursor — Gmail historyId, Calendar syncToken, Drive pageToken — which is only moved after the upsert commits, so a crash reprocesses rather than skips.

202 with a task id per service. Nothing here is a 409: a service that is already running or whose circuit breaker is open comes back in `skipped` with a reason.

exec: pm.test('queued or plainly skipped, never an error', function () {

request.description: Continues the historical walk from backfill_cursor over SYNC_BACKFILL_DAYS (180). Separate from the incremental cursor so the two never fight.
Discards the cursor and re-walks from scratch. Expensive, and rate limited to once an hour per service — a second attempt inside the hour is 429 with Retry-After.

exec: pm.test('202, or 429 if you already did this within the hour', function () {

request.description:
lag_seconds is now - last_success_at, which is why last_success_at exists separately from last_synced_at: a failing sync updates the attempt but not the success, and the lag figure must reflect the data rather than the effort.

within_target:false is the honest report that the mirror is staler than the 15-minute goal. In that window a superlative query ('my next flight') should pass freshness:'live' rather than trust the mirror.

exec: pm.test('lag is derived from last_success_at, not last_synced_at', function () {

item.name: 7 · Search (debug and eval)
item.description: The retrieval layer with the lid off. Not on the chat path — this is for debugging a bad answer and for the offline Precision@5 run. It returns every score component so you can see why something ranked where it did.

request.description:
One embedding, three parallel hybrid searches: metadata prefilter (always user_id) then vector cosine in parallel with Postgres full-text, fused with RRF k=60 FOR ORDERING ONLY, then temporal decay exp(-age_days/30) for mail and a forward boost for future events.

The floors are computed on `cn` (cosine normalised per corpus, z-scored, clamped 0..1) plus an evidence flag — NEVER on the fused RRF score, because RRF is rank-derived and cannot tell a perfect match from the best of three bad ones.

exec: pm.test('every hit shows its score components', function () {
pm.test('the decision is made on cn, not on rrf', function () {
pm.test('the verdict is one of three', function () {

request.description: The attendee prefilter is a GIN index hit on sync_items.participant_emails — a generated column over the participants JSONB, so participants stays the single source and this stays an index scan.

Metadata prefilter before the vector scan — cheaper than filtering after, and the reason 'PDFs from last month' is fast. Remember a file row has no created date, so the date window is on occurred_at, which holds Drive's modified time.

freshness=live reads through to Google before searching, for when the mirror's 15-minute lag is not good enough. Slower, and honest about it in took_ms. This is the only mode that can return 428 or 503.

item.name: 8 · Health
item.description: At the root, not under /api/v1 — a load balancer should not have to know your API version. None of these need a session.

request.description: Answers from process memory and touches nothing. It only fails by not answering, which is exactly what a liveness probe should mean.

Checks postgres, the pgvector extension, redis, celery and the migration head in parallel with a 500ms budget each.

A failed celery check reports ok:false but does NOT fail readiness — the API serves reads without a worker, and pulling the whole tier out of the load balancer because a queue is down turns a degradation into an outage.
